newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israeli firms to hold first trade fair in Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Israeli firms to hold first trade fair in Jordan.

text.p: The first Israeli trade exhibition in Jordan will be held in Amman next month despite a strong climate of business hostility over commercial ties with the Jewish state, Jordanian organisers said on Friday.

"If we stay reserved and they stay reserved...until when will this situation last?" Fakhri Al-Naser, general manager of Jordanian International and National Expo Corporation, the organiser of the exibition, told Reuters.
Naser said more than 80 Israeli companies had already booked a total of between 1,500-2,000 square metres of display space in the exhibition hall of the Jordan Export Promotion Fair.

More than 250 Israeli businessmen are expected to attend the four-day exhibition which will start on December 15 and display a wide range of Israeli output, including high tech products, garments, jewellery, chemicals and furniture.

Naser said the fair had the support of key Israeli governmental agencies, including the Israeli Export Institute, which had given their blessing for Israeli companies to participate despite heightened Middle East tension that has soured the climate for expanding Arab-Israeli business deals.

Arab Gulf businessmen will also show up at the fair despite misgivings over premature deals with Israeli firms before there is a comprehensive Middle East peace. They were "very interested in getting familiarised with Israeli products," Naser said.

A planned exhibition of Jordanian products in Tel Aviv next March had drawn interest by Jordanian firms keen on exploring the Israeli market for their products and also having a foothold in the lucrative Palestinian market, he said.

But many leading Jordanian businessmen continue to shun contact with Israeli firms despite normalised trade ties after Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, saying such ties are premature as long as Israel continues to hold on to captured Arab land.
They believe making deals now would give Israel a bounty it does not deserve before it delivers on its peace pledges.

The few who have business dealings say renewed Arab-Israeli hatreds have made them freeze plans, or rethink them in what they describe as an inhospitable climate, forbidding open contact despite official blessing.
